=========== ed5f8e17c
Stefan Haubold | 2026-08-20
fix(trail): push a trail branch to the branch's push remote, not origin

`entire trail create` delivered the trail's branch with a hardcoded
`origin` in four places — push, ls-remote, fetch, and the cleanup
delete — plus the `git push origin --delete` hint. In any repo whose
branch pushes somewhere else (a fork workflow holding the upstream as
origin, or any repo with remote.pushDefault set) the branch went to the
wrong remote and nothing warned.

Delivery now resolves through git's own precedence via
strategy.DeclaredPushRemoteForBranch, falling back to origin. The
resolve happens once in runTrailCreate, next to the sibling
resolveTrailRemote, and the name is threaded down, so push and cleanup
cannot disagree about where the branch went. A branch being newly
created has no branch.<name>.* config, so it resolves through
remote.pushDefault to origin: unchanged for the common case.

Reads the declaration for the target branch rather than HEAD, so
`trail create --branch other` does not inherit the current branch's
push remote.

A declared name starting with "-" is rejected rather than silently
retargeted at origin. Deliberately not validateGitRemoteName: that
whitelist vets names Entire is about to write into .git/config and is
stricter than git, so against config the user already has it rejects
values git accepts wherever a <repository> goes — "." and a bare URL
both fail its leading-alphanumeric rule.

The four wrappers now take ctx and derive their timeouts from it; they
each built context.Background() internally, so Ctrl-C during a
two-minute push was ignored.

remoteHasBranch is named to avoid shadowing the exported
BranchExistsOnRemote by case alone. They are not merged: that one is
origin-only and reports an ls-remote failure as "branch absent", which
here would mark the branch as ours and let cleanup delete a branch the
user already had.

Scope: delivery only. resolveTrailRemote still reads the trail's
forge/owner/repo from origin, so the two can name different repos in a
fork setup, and a repo with no origin at all fails there first. The
fetch side (trail checkout) still hardcodes origin.

Tests cover the tier table, the origin fallback, target-branch-not-HEAD,
the flag rejection, a legal "." remote, and an end-to-end push that must
land on the declared remote and not leak to origin. They isolate global
git config, without which a developer carrying remote.pushDefault fails
the fallback case.

## Short answer

Nobody wrote down a reason, and the session that would have explained it is gone.

## Where it came from

`--no-verify` was on the trail-branch push from the very first line of code that pushed one:

**`6e687f70c`** — "Push branch and trail data to origin after trail create", Daniel Adams, 2026-02-23, on `feat/trails`, co-authored by Claude Opus 4.6.

```go
// pushBranchToOrigin pushes a branch to the origin remote.
func pushBranchToOrigin(branchName string) error {
	cmd := exec.CommandContext(ctx, "git", "push", "--no-verify", "-u", "origin", branchName)
```

The commit message says only: *"pushes the new branch to origin (with -u for tracking) and syncs the trails metadata branch. Push failures are non-blocking warnings."* No mention of hooks, no code comment, nothing about why verification is skipped.

## The session is unrecoverable

`entire checkpoint explain 6e687f70c07d08a010d74c745e21b1841dd04335` →

```
commit 6e687f7 references checkpoint 18e798499438 via its
Entire-Checkpoint trailer: checkpoint not found: 18e798499438
```

A dangling trailer. Same for all four sibling commits from that same day's `feat/trails` run (`fc76ba4ab962`, `0c1e138e4ae0`, `ff63e394e0c2`, `73308b5a6ad8`) — none of them resolve, while other people's 2026-02-23 checkpoints *are* present in the published v1 history. So it's specific to that branch's run, not a retention cutoff.

Which is the joke: the reasoning for `--no-verify` was lost to a branch whose checkpoints never got pushed — the bug class trail 1219 is fixing.

## The only reason the code itself supports

This is inference from the diff, not documentation. The same commit pushed Entire's data itself, on the very next lines:

```go
if err := strategy.PushTrailsBranch("origin"); err != nil {
	fmt.Fprintf(errW, "Warning: failed to push trail data: %v\n", err)
}
```

So the author's model looks like *"I push the branch, then I push Entire's data myself"* — and `--no-verify` skipped what appeared to be a duplicate job. But `PushTrailsBranch` was `pushSessionsBranchCommon(remote, paths.TrailsBranchName)`: the **trails metadata branch only**. It never touched checkpoint/session refs. The substitution was incomplete on day one, and that's precisely the gap trail 1219 closes six months later.

## Then it survived four rewrites unexamined

`1a6c8a505` (Jun 17, copied the flag onto the delete path) → `dc40fb68c2e9` (Jun 18, made the push a *hard precondition*) → `1fd4f9fdd` (Jun 18) → `ed5f8e17c` (Aug 20, your rewrite of remote resolution, with a very thorough message). None of them mention `--no-verify`. Daniel's agent in the fix session ran the same archaeology I did (`git log -S`, `git blame`, `git show 6e687f70c0`) and also came up empty — which is why `14107d1be` just asserts the new invariant instead of refuting an old rationale:

```go
// resolveTrailPushRemote rather than assuming "origin". This must run Git's
// pre-push hooks: Entire's hook publishes any checkpoint data that was captured
// before the trail branch was created.
```

## One thing worth separating out

There *is* a legitimate, documented `--no-verify` nearby — `setup_github.go:1055`, on the first push of a brand-new repo, so `entire/checkpoints/v1` isn't pushed alongside the default branch (GitHub can otherwise pick it as the default). Real reason, different situation; it never applied to trail create. If anyone tries to justify the trail one retroactively, that's the argument they'll reach for, and it doesn't hold.

Also still on main after the fix: `deleteBranchFromRemote` (`trail_cmd.go:2450`) keeps `--no-verify`. Probably right for a delete push, but it's the last copy of the pattern and it's still undocumented.

## Review of trail 1219

The one-line fix is correct and the comment states the invariant well. But the diff stops one step short: it makes the hook *run* without making its output *reach the user*, and that turns out to matter a lot.

### 1. The hook now runs, but its output and its prompts are captured and discarded — high

`pushBranchToRemote` still uses `cmd.CombinedOutput()`, and that buffer is only read to build an error string. Everything the pre-push hook says lands in it:

| what | where it writes |
| --- | --- |
| `[entire] Pushing N checkpoint ref(s) to origin...` | `manual_commit_push.go:491` → `os.Stderr` |
| `warnOPFCheckpointRefsWithheld` | `manual_commit_push.go:272` → `stderrWriter` = `os.Stderr` (`manual_commit_hooks.go:821`) |
| `askOPFPrompt`'s huh form | `uiform.New` → huh defaults to `os.Stdout` / `os.Stdin` |

Three consequences:

**(a)** On success the user sees nothing. `entire trail create` prints `Pushed branch X to origin` and that's it — the checkpoint sync this change exists to trigger is invisible.

**(b)** On the **git-refs** backend, an OPF failure calls `warnOPFCheckpointRefsWithheld`, returns false, and `PrePushFromGitHook` still returns nil — the push succeeds with the refs left queued. So trail create reports success while the checkpoints stay local. That is the original bug, unfixed, with its only warning now suppressed.

**(c)** The OPF prompt. `CanPromptInteractively()` decides purely from a `/dev/tty` probe (`interactive/interactive.go:55`) — it never looks at stdin or stdout. So for a human in a terminal with OPF on and `prompt_default` unset, `hasTTY` is true and `askOPFPrompt` renders a Bubble Tea form into a pipe with `/dev/null` for input. Whatever that resolves to decides whether the push aborts (`errOPFAbortedByUser`, `manual_commit_push.go:149`, git-branch) or the refs are withheld (git-refs).

Fix: stream rather than capture — `cmd.Stdout`/`cmd.Stderr` wired to the command's writers, exit status kept for the error. That's what "push like a user would" actually means.

Worth noting *why* this got missed: the dev loop ran through Pi, and `PI_CODING_AGENT` trips `isAgentSubprocessEnv()` → `hasTTY` false → OPF auto-runs with a progress line instead of a prompt. The human path is the one with no coverage.

### 2. The hard-failure path is new, untested, and its hint now misleads — medium

`prepareTrailCreateBranch:1126` treats a push failure as fatal: cleanup runs, trail creation aborts. Before this change the push could only fail on network/auth. Now **any** non-zero pre-push exit kills trail creation — Entire's OPF abort, or the user's own pre-push hook running tests or lint. Meanwhile the hint still reads:

```
- if this is an auth error, link your GitHub account and retry
- if this is a non-fast-forward, update branch %q from %q and retry
```

...with the real cause sitting in the captured buffer. Either widen the hint, or don't treat a hook rejection as a delivery failure at all.

A negative test is ~10 lines beside the new one: `pre-push` that `exit 1` → assert the error and that cleanup ran.

### 3. The 2-minute timeout now bounds hook work too — medium

`pushBranchToRemote` keeps `2*time.Minute`. That used to bound a network push; it now also bounds OPF re-redaction (~30s advertised, and the bootstrap case walks all unpushed history) plus the checkpoint ref pushes. On expiry `exec.CommandContext` kills git mid-hook. Either raise it or say why 2 minutes still holds.

### 4. `deleteBranchFromRemote` keeps `--no-verify`, undocumented — low

Line 2450. Probably correct — you don't want checkpoint sync on a branch delete — but the new comment asserts "This must run Git's pre-push hooks" without saying why its sibling must not. One clause there stops the next person removing it for consistency.

Related new state: if the push succeeds (hook publishes refs) and trail creation then fails, cleanup deletes the branch while the checkpoint refs stay published. Harmless, since they were meant to be pushed, but it's new.

### 5. Drop the `contexts_test.go` line — low

`t.Fatal` calls `runtime.Goexit()`, so the added `return` is unreachable and guards nothing. I ran `mise run lint` on clean main: **0 issues** — so it isn't silencing a linter either. And the commit carrying it is titled "Fix nil guard in contexts test", which describes something the line doesn't do. Unrelated file, no effect; cut it.

### What's right

- Correct fix, and the comment explains the invariant rather than just restating the code.
- The test isolates global git config via `testutil.IsolateGitConfigEnv` (`initTrailCleanupRepo:349`) — without that, a developer carrying a global `core.hooksPath` gets a false failure.
- Asserting `$1 == "origin"` ties it to the remote resolution from `ed5f8e17c` instead of just "a hook ran".
- No recursion hazard: the checkpoint push itself passes `--no-verify` (`checkpoint/remote/git.go:434`).

### One coverage note

`TestGitPushWithHooks_SyncsCheckpointsToRemote` already exists in `integration_test/real_hook_push_test.go`, and `testenv.GitPushWithHooks` is right there. The new unit test asserts a proxy (some hook fired); an integration test asserting real checkpoint refs land after `trail create` would assert the actual claim. No — three things, and the third is the one that makes the push non-negotiable.

**1. The ref has to exist before the create request.** `newTrailCreateRequest` sets `BranchAction = "link"` unconditionally whenever a branch is named (`trail_cmd.go:1219`). Per `dc40fb68c2e9`, without the branch on the remote the server "had no remote branch to anchor to and backfilled it at the base tip, producing local/remote/work drift while still printing 'Created trail'."

**2. Not just the ref — the commits.** The trail's `headSha` is the delivered tip (1219's is `a9e95a1b`). If the branch already exists on the remote but is behind, the push has to fast-forward it — that's what the non-fast-forward branch of the error hint is for. So it's a content delivery, not a ref creation.

**3. `-u` sets tracking.** Purely local, but it's what makes the next bare `git push` from that branch work — and, neatly, what lets `strategy.DeclaredPushRemoteForBranch` resolve on subsequent pushes, which is the machinery `ed5f8e17c` added.

## The point I think you're circling

Checkpoint publication is not a *purpose* of that push. It's a side effect of a hook the push happens to trigger. So the fix couples "publish checkpoints" to "deliver a branch" through a hook, on a push the user never typed, whose stdout is a buffer and whose stdin is `/dev/null`.

And the irony: the original commit had the right architecture and the wrong function. It *did* push Entire's data explicitly, on the very next lines —

```go
if err := strategy.PushTrailsBranch("origin"); err != nil {
```

— it just pushed the trails metadata branch instead of the checkpoint refs. The fix inverts that: rather than correcting the explicit call, it deletes the flag and adopts the hook as the mechanism.

I still think removing `--no-verify` is the better of the two. One code path, no drift, and the hook is the only thing that knows the whole push story — which refs are queued, which remote is elected, whether OPF applies, the policy sync. An explicit call would have to re-derive all of that and would rot.

Five findings. Two were right and I've fixed them; the High one is wrong on its stated mechanism.

## The High finding is wrong — `01M1Y6WD9BEP`

> Git push hooks run **after** the network transfer, so a hook rejection leaves an orphaned branch on the remote.

That premise is false for `pre-push` — rejecting is the whole point of it. Tested directly:

```
--- push (hook rejects) ---
    hook ran, rejecting
    error: failed to push some refs to '../origin.git'
--- refs on the remote afterwards ---
    ref count: 0
```

The branch never lands. `TestPrepareTrailCreateBranchFailsWhenPrePushHookRejects`, already on the branch, asserts exactly this and passes.

There *is* a narrow residual behind it: `cleanupCreatedTrailBranch` is called with a hardcoded `false` for `remotePushed` (`trail_cmd.go:1140`), so if the push landed refs and *then* errored — a SIGKILL at the timeout is the only realistic route — the remote branch is orphaned. That `false` predates this trail, and the suggested `state.RemotePushed || existedOnRemote` would be wrong: `existedOnRemote` means the user already had the branch, so cleanup would delete a branch we didn't create. Not fixing it here — narrow, pre-existing, and changing cleanup semantics is a call for the branch owner.

## Fixed — `01M1XX4E1ENC` (stdin), right in direction

I'd written that inheriting stdin lets git prompt for credentials. That justification doesn't hold: `git push` has no `--stdin`, the hook gets git's ref-list pipe rather than ours, the OPF prompt reads `/dev/tty` via bubbletea's fallback, and git's credential prompt uses `/dev/tty`/askpass. So the only effect was replacing an immediate EOF with a real blocking read — an agent-driven `trail create` could hang for ten minutes instead of failing fast. Dropped; stdin stays at `/dev/null`.

## Fixed — `01M1Y5JYARYN`, even though it's marked dismissed

It's technically right, and there's a repo-idiomatic fix nobody applied. `exec.CommandContext`'s default `Cancel` kills only the direct child — and the pre-push hook is a *grandchild*. So a timeout orphaned it: `trail create` returns an error while a detached hook keeps rewriting checkpoint refs behind it. Now using `execx.TerminateOnCancel`, which kills the process group and sets `WaitDelay`.

The finding's literal complaint — SIGKILL corrupting a mid-ref-write — has no fix at this layer, and I said so in the comment rather than implying otherwise. But an orphaned writer nobody is waiting for is strictly worse than a stopped one.
